shadcn/ui is a collection of re-usable components that you can copy and paste into your apps. It is not a traditional component library. Instead, it provides you with the source code for each component, allowing you to customize and integrate them directly into your project.

Use shadcn/ui when you want full control over your components and prefer to customize them to fit your specific design requirements. It's suitable for projects where you want to avoid the overhead of a large component library and prefer a more hands-on approach.

Avoid shadcn/ui if you prefer a component library with pre-built themes and styles that require minimal customization. Also, if you're not comfortable with manually integrating and maintaining individual components, shadcn/ui might not be the best choice.

shadcn has 64 components, 44 of them are unique – for example pagination and button group are considered as same.
Does not support more than 2 themes at the same time
Imported JavaScript bundle size (minified) of dependencies installed by shadcn CLI

shadcn CLI installs 159 third-party dependencies (Not including React and Tailwind CSS). Using more third-party dependencies increases the risk of security vulnerabilities, compatibility problems, and long-term maintenance headaches from deprecated packages.
shadcn CSS file is not available on CDN
shadcn does not use semantic CSS class names. Using semantic and descriptive CSS class names improves readability and maintainability of code independent of the current framework.
shadcn requires changing JavaScript props one by one at build time to do design token customization
shadcn does not provide micro CSS files for each component
shadcn does not use wide-gamut P3 colors by default
shadcn does not supports right-to-left (RTL) layouts by default
shadcn customizations requires changing JavaScript props at build time
shadcn doesn not use native CSS nesting
Components are installed individually via the CLI tool rather than as a package. This requires installing more dependencies for each component.

shadcn components exist in your codebase meaning you should manually maintain, debug and develop them. They will not receive updates and bug fixes  automatically .Updating them manually according to shadcn changes means resetting all your customizations on each update.

shadcn works as a registry of components, rather than a library. The CLI tool generates component files in your project. After that, there's no versioning, no updates, and no compatibility guarantees between components.

daisyUI is a component library for Tailwind CSS that provides pre-designed components with theming capabilities. It is framework-agnostic, meaning it can be used in any web project, and it doesn't ship any JavaScript to the browser.

Use daisyUI when you want to rapidly prototype or build a project with a consistent design system based on Tailwind CSS. It's well-suited for projects where you need a large variety of customizable components and theme options without writing a lot of custom CSS.

Avoid daisyUI if you need highly specific or unique component designs that deviate significantly from the pre-designed styles. Also, if you prefer to build all components from scratch for maximum control over every detail, daisyUI might not be the best choice.
daisyUI is framework agnostic and works everywhere
daisyUI has 68 components, 65 of them are unique – for example pagination and button group are considered as same.
daisyUI supports unlimited themes at the same time, allowing for dynamic theme switching.
daisyUI doesn't ship JavaScript to browsers
daisyUI has no dependencies. It's immune to 3rd party vulnerabilities, dependency version mismatch, and deprecation issues.
In GitHub's top 400 repositories of all time
daisyUI CSS file is available on CDN
daisyUI uses semantic CSS class names. Using semantic and descriptive CSS class names improves readability and maintainability of code independent of the current framework.
daisyUI provides tokens, root-level CSS variables and component-level CSS variables that let you adjust colors, sizes, spacing, radius, and other styles to match your design.
daisyUI can be used as a standalone file, with Tailwind CSS standalone version. This is useful for projects without a Node.js environment.
daisyUI provides micro CSS files for each component
daisyUI uses CSS variables for design customization at runtime
daisyUI uses native CSS nesting, reducing the CSS file size
Choosing between daisyUI and shadcn/ui for a production UI

Choosing a shadcn/ui alternative is less about chasing one metric and more about how the library fits your project over time. The data gives a useful starting point: 65 daisyUI components versus 44 in shadcn/ui, 35 built-in daisyUI themes versus 2, and 0 daisyUI dependencies versus 159 for shadcn/ui. daisyUI is built around Tailwind CSS classes, CSS variables, and framework-agnostic HTML, so the UI layer stays portable while your app keeps its own JavaScript behavior.

shadcn/ui gives you 44 unique components. daisyUI gives you 65, but the larger difference is how those components are used: they are class names you can apply to normal HTML instead of a separate component API you have to wrap, import, or adapt.

shadcn/ui lists 2 built-in themes. daisyUI includes 35, and the theme system is based on CSS variables, so you can switch themes at runtime, keep dark mode simple, and customize colors without rewriting every component.

shadcn/ui has a JavaScript size of 2000kB, while daisyUI is 0. That matters when a page only needs styling. daisyUI lets your framework handle state and interaction while the component styles stay in CSS.

shadcn/ui is built for Only React. daisyUI works across ALL because it styles HTML with Tailwind CSS classes. That makes it easier to use the same design language in React, Vue, Svelte, server-rendered templates, static HTML, or a mixed stack.

shadcn/ui can be the right choice when you want its exact component model. daisyUI is stronger when you want Tailwind CSS control, semantic component classes, runtime CSS variables, P3 colors, RTL support, and native CSS features without locking the markup to one framework.
GitHub stars are only one signal, but daisyUI has a large enough count to show real community pull. NPM usage gives daisyUI a measurable adoption signal, even when another library has a larger count.

NPM usage gives daisyUI a measurable adoption signal, even when another library has a larger count.
daisyUI's component count is higher than shadcn/ui's, which helps teams build complete screens with fewer gaps.
The package stands on its own as a Tailwind CSS plugin, so there is less to reconcile during upgrades.
The main difference is ownership. With daisyUI, your Tailwind CSS setup owns the styling system. With shadcn/ui, more of the UI behavior and structure usually comes from the library.
